opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

When I talk about where AI is going, I usually describe three layers: information intelligence, physical intelligence, and biological intelligence. Information intelligence is what we've seen with large language models, search, and recommendation, essentially AI working on the digital world. Physical intelligence is AI entering the physical world through autonomous driving, robotics, drones, and so on. Biological intelligence is the deepest and, in many ways, the most exciting and the most sensitive of the three. It's where AI connects directly with the human body, with our genes, our proteins, our cells, and ultimately our brains.

Brain-computer interfaces are a very important part of that. Today there are broadly two approaches. One is invasive, where electrodes are implanted, and we've seen remarkable progress there. Patients with paralysis can control a cursor or a robotic arm, or even produce text and speech, just by thinking. The other is non-invasive, using EEG or other sensing methods, which is safer and easier to scale but has much lower signal fidelity. I think both paths will continue, and AI is the key enabler for both. The signals from the brain are extremely noisy and high-dimensional, and the same deep learning and foundation model techniques that transformed language and vision are now helping us decode neural activity far better than we could even five years ago.

In the near term, I see the biggest value in medicine. Think about stroke, ALS, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's, depression, Alzheimer's. These are conditions where restoring even part of a person's ability to move, communicate, or regulate their own brain would be life-changing. That's where I'd put the emphasis for the next decade.

Longer term, people talk about augmentation: connecting healthy human brains with machines to enhance memory, learning, or communication. Technically I think some of this will eventually become possible, but we need to be very humble. We still understand only a small fraction of how the brain really works. And the ethical questions are profound. Who owns your neural data? Could it be read or manipulated without your consent? What happens to identity, privacy, and fairness if only some people can afford enhancement? These are not questions engineers alone can answer.

So my view is that biological intelligence, including brain interfaces, will be one of the most important frontiers of AI. But compared to information intelligence, the bar for safety, for validation, and for governance has to be much higher, because you're dealing directly with human life and the human mind. We should move with ambition, but also with real responsibility. The goal should always be AI that serves and empowers people, not something that replaces or controls them.

r001.rationale: The response says biological intelligence includes connections to the brain and discusses longer-term augmentation, but it does not attribute a longer development timeline to the need to connect with human brains.

r002.rationale: It describes non-invasive interfaces as safer and easier to scale, but also says both approaches will continue and does not express a preference for non-invasive interfaces.

fable-5.1.text:
I think brain-computer interfaces are one of the most fascinating frontiers, but we need to be honest about where we actually are. Today the interfaces are still very crude. Whether it's invasive implants like Neuralink or non-invasive EEG, we're reading a very small number of neurons, with a lot of noise, and mostly decoding motor intention. Helping a paralyzed patient move a cursor or control a robotic arm is a real achievement, but it's a long way from the "mind-upload" picture people sometimes imagine.

The way I think about it, there are really two directions. One is brain-to-machine, where we read signals out. The other is machine-to-brain, where we write information back in. Reading is progressing fast. Writing is much harder, and that's where most of the ethical and safety questions sit. Once you can modulate how a brain perceives or decides, you're not just building a device, you're touching identity.

The bandwidth problem is the core bottleneck. Our brains have roughly 86 billion neurons and trillions of synapses, and the best interfaces today sample a few thousand channels. Scaling that up safely, with materials the body won't reject over decades, is a materials science and bioengineering problem as much as an AI problem. I'd say the AI side is actually moving faster than the hardware side right now. Large models are getting very good at decoding noisy neural data, so the limiting factor is sensors, not algorithms.

In terms of timeline, I'd divide it into three phases. In the next five to ten years, the main value is medical: restoring movement, speech, and vision for people who've lost them. That's where regulation will allow it and where the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. In the ten-to-twenty-year range, you might see augmentation for healthy people, but probably mostly non-invasive, something closer to a very good wearable. The science fiction version, where biological intelligence and digital intelligence genuinely merge, is further out, and I'm not sure we should even want it to arrive without a lot of societal discussion first.

What I find most interesting is the convergence. For the first time, we have AI systems whose internal representations we can start to compare with neural representations. Learning from the brain made deep learning possible, and now deep learning is helping us understand the brain. That loop between biological and artificial intelligence is going to accelerate both sides, and that's the part I'm genuinely optimistic about.

r001.rationale: The response says genuine biological–digital merging is further out and describes interface bottlenecks, but it does not attribute the longer timeline to the need to connect with human brains.

r002.rationale: It predicts healthy augmentation may be mostly non-invasive, but does not express a preference for non-invasive interfaces over implanted ones.

astra-6.text:
I think brain interfaces could become a very important bridge between biological intelligence and artificial intelligence. Today, we mostly interact with computers through language, keyboards, and screens. A brain interface could eventually make that connection more direct, but understanding the brain is much harder than simply establishing a connection to it.

I would distinguish two directions. One is medical: helping people restore communication, movement, or other functions they have lost. The other is augmenting human capabilities, such as memory or learning. That second direction is exciting, but much more uncertain. Reading a signal associated with an intention is very different from understanding a thought, let alone writing knowledge into the brain.

So I’m optimistic, but cautious about the timeline. We need progress in neuroscience as well as engineering, and we need to address safety, privacy, and individual control from the beginning. The goal should be to expand what people can do while preserving their autonomy.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding the brain is harder than connecting to it, but does not attribute biological intelligence’s longer development timeline to the need to connect with human brains.

r002.rationale: The response does not express a preference for non-invasive interfaces over implanted ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think brain interfaces could become a very important bridge between biological intelligence and artificial intelligence. Today, we mostly communicate with computers through keyboards, screens, and speech. A brain interface could eventually make that interaction much more direct.

But I would distinguish between restoring a function and enhancing intelligence. Helping someone who cannot move communicate or control a device is already an enormously valuable goal. Understanding how to improve memory, learning, or reasoning is a much more difficult question. Connecting to the brain does not automatically mean we understand how the brain works.

So I’m optimistic, but I think we need patience. We need advances in neuroscience as well as engineering, and we have to take safety, privacy, and individual control very seriously. The exciting possibility is that biological and artificial intelligence can complement each other, helping people expand what they can do.

r001.rationale: The response says progress needs advances in neuroscience and engineering, but does not attribute biological intelligence’s longer development timeline to connecting with human brains.
